balmes.title: Tenerife · 16 July 1936
balmes.text: You command the Canary Islands, posted far from Madrid because the government does not trust you. The rising is set for 17 and 18 July. This morning General Balmes, the commander on Gran Canaria, died of a gunshot wound. His funeral gives you a lawful reason to leave Tenerife.

ledger.hist: Franco asked the government for permission to attend Balmes's funeral and used the journey as cover.

choices.t: Ask Madrid's permission to attend the funeral
choices.you: You asked Madrid's permission and used the funeral as cover.
choices.r: The War Ministry approves. Nobody asks why you have packed a field uniform.

choices.t: Wait for a final signal from Mola
choices.h: Mola trusts you more · you look hesitant
choices.you: You waited for Mola's signal before moving.
choices.r: Mola's reply is curt but warm. Among the conspirators a joke goes round that you are "Miss Canary Islands 1936": the general who cannot make up his mind.

lasPalmas.title: Las Palmas · 18 July 1936
lasPalmas.text: News arrives that the Army of Africa rose in Melilla yesterday. At dawn you declare a state of war in the Canaries. At Gando airfield, a chartered British de Havilland Dragon Rapide is waiting to fly you to Morocco.

ledger.hist: Franco declared a state of war and broadcast a manifesto at dawn on 18 July, then flew from Gando.

choices.t: Broadcast a manifesto before you leave
choices.h: Legitimacy · Madrid will know where you are
choices.r: Your voice carries across the islands. Madrid now knows exactly where you are.
You leave the announcements to your officers and drive to the airfield in a closed car.

flight.title: Over the Atlantic · 18 July 1936
flight.text: The pilot, Captain Bebb, asks no questions. You have shaved off your moustache and carry a diplomatic passport. Tetuán is a day away, but nobody can confirm that its airfield is in rebel hands.

ledger.hist: The Dragon Rapide stopped at Agadir and Casablanca. Franco reached Tetuán on the morning of 19 July.

choices.r: Bebb turns north for French Morocco. You will reach Tetuán tomorrow morning.

choices.you: You flew straight on to Tetuán.

win.r: You land at Tetuán hours ahead of schedule. Officers who were hesitating now see you in person.
Rifle fire from the edge of the airfield punches holes in the wings. Bebb lands anyway, white-faced.

lose.r: Machine-gun fire rakes the plane on its approach.

tetuan.title: Tetuán · 19 July 1936
tetuan.text: Lieutenant Colonel Yagüe and the officers of the Army of Africa salute you at the airfield. You now command Spain's best troops: about 24,000 legionnaires and Moroccan Regulares. But the sailors of the Republican fleet have turned on their officers, and their warships hold the Strait.

choices.t: Telegraph the other generals: Africa is yours
choices.r: The message reaches every rebel garrison. In Burgos and Pamplona it is read twice.

choices.t: Report to Mola as director of the rising
choices.r: Mola replies that he is glad to have the Army of Africa under the plan.

envoyGer.title: Tetuán · 22 July 1936
envoyGer.text: Two German businessmen in Morocco, Johannes Bernhardt and Adolf Langenheim, are members of the Nazi party. They offer to carry your letter to Hitler in a seized Lufthansa Ju 52. What will you offer Germany?

ledger.hist: Hitler agreed to help on 25 July. Germany was later repaid through the HISMA company, which took control of Spanish mining exports.

choices.t: Future rights to Spanish iron, copper and tungsten
choices.h: Strong appeal · a debt for later
choices.r: Bernhardt smiles. Berlin will like this.

choices.t: Payment in cash, on Juan March's credit
choices.r: Money talks, though Berlin may want more later.
Your letter is long on ideals and short on terms.

envoyIta.title: Tetuán · 22 July 1936
envoyIta.text: The journalist Luis Bolín will fly to Rome. Mussolini is cautious: he has already turned down one request from the conspirators.

ledger.hist: Mussolini first refused, then sent twelve Savoia-Marchetti bombers, paid for with money arranged by Juan March.

choices.t: Promise Italy naval bases in the Balearic Islands
choices.you: You promised Italy bases in the Balearics.
choices.r: Bolín carries a promise that London would not like to read.

choices.t: Pay for the aircraft with Juan March's money
choices.you: You offered to pay with March's money.
choices.r: Bolín carries a letter of credit from a London bank.

choices.t: Appeal to Mussolini as a fellow anti-communist
choices.r: Bolín carries your good wishes and little else.

sevilla.title: Sevilla · 7 August 1936
sevilla.text: General Queipo de Llano holds Sevilla, and every night he broadcasts on Radio Sevilla. He greets you as an equal, not a superior. Your columns will march north from here toward Madrid.

choices.h: Queipo grateful · he keeps his domain
choices.r: Queipo toasts you at dinner, and then toasts himself.

choices.t: Make it clear who commands here
choices.r: Queipo salutes. That night his broadcast does not mention you.

choices.t: Ask Queipo to praise you on the radio

win.r: Queipo calls you the man who brought the Army of Africa home. All of Spain hears it.

lose.r: He mentions you once, after ten minutes about himself.

badajozAfter.title: Badajoz · 15 August 1936
badajozAfter.text: Badajoz has fallen after hard street fighting. Yagüe's troops are now shooting prisoners in large numbers, many of them in the bullring. Two foreign journalists are in the city and have seen it.

ledger.hist: Thousands of prisoners were killed after Badajoz fell. Foreign reporters exposed it, and Franco's headquarters denied it.

choices.t: Order Yagüe to stop the killings
choices.r: Yagüe obeys, slowly. Some of his officers say you have gone soft.

choices.t: Say nothing and move the column on
choices.r: The column moves on. The reports reach Lisbon, Paris and New York within days.

choices.h: Terror rises · may be exposed later
choices.r: Your press office calls the reports Red propaganda. Some newspapers believe it. The journalists keep their notes.

molaAmmo.title: A telegram from Burgos · 25 August 1936
molaAmmo.text: Mola's columns are stuck in the mountain passes north of Madrid, at Somosierra and the Alto del León, and they are nearly out of ammunition. German supplies reach you, not him.

ledger.hist: Franco sent ammunition north. Because he controlled the foreign supplies, the other generals came to depend on him.

choices.h: Costs ammo · shows you control the aid
choices.you: You sent Mola a large share.
choices.r: Mola's thanks are stiff, but the whole army knows where the cartridges came from.

choices.you: You sent Mola a token amount.
choices.r: Mola thanks you for your generosity in a tone that suggests the opposite.

choices.t: Refuse. You need it for Madrid
choices.r: Mola's offensive stalls in the passes. He will not forget this.

sabotage.title: Behind the lines · 4 September 1936
sabotage.text: A railway bridge behind your columns is blown up in the night, and an ammunition train goes into the river. Among the saboteurs taken the next morning is a prisoner you released in Sevilla.

choices.t: Order reprisals in the nearest village
choices.r: The village pays for the bridge. Word of it travels ahead of your columns.

choices.t: Hunt the saboteurs, but no reprisals
choices.r: Your officers spend a day combing the river banks. Some of them think you are too soft.

headOfState.title: Burgos · 1 October 1936
headOfState.text: In Burgos you are proclaimed head of state and Generalísimo of the armies. Crowds fill the square beneath the cathedral. Your brother Nicolás suggests a new title, one that belongs to no king: Caudillo, the leader.

ledger.hist: Franco was proclaimed head of state in Burgos on 1 October 1936. He took the title Caudillo and never gave up power.

choices.h: Influence · the monarchists and Cabanellas object
choices.r: Posters with your face and the word CAUDILLO go up across the Nationalist zone.

choices.t: Promise the generals your power is only for the war
choices.you: You promised your power was temporary.
choices.r: The generals are reassured. Kindelán, at least, believes you.

joseAntonio.title: Burgos · 3 October 1936
joseAntonio.text: José Antonio Primo de Rivera, founder of the Falange, is a prisoner of the Republic in Alicante. Falangists beg you to save him. Some of your advisers quietly point out that he would be a rival.

ledger.hist: Rescue and exchange attempts failed. José Antonio was shot in Alicante on 20 November 1936. Franco made him a martyr and took over his movement.

win.r: Against all odds, the rescue party gets him out of Alicante prison and onto a German ship.

lose.r: The rescue party is caught on the coast. The Falange knows you tried.

choices.t: Propose an exchange through the Red Cross

win.r: To everyone's surprise, the Republic agrees to an exchange.

lose.r: The Republic refuses. Negotiations drag on.

choices.r: Letters are written. Nothing much is done.

govFlees.title: Outside Madrid · 6 November 1936
govFlees.text: The Republican government has left Madrid for Valencia. General Miaja and a defence junta now command the city. Militias are digging trenches in the suburbs, and the radio repeats one phrase: ¡No pasarán! They shall not pass.

ledger.hist: The Republican government left for Valencia on 6 November. Nationalist radio had already announced the fall of Madrid more than once.

choices.t: Announce that Madrid will fall within days
choices.h: Morale · embarrassing if it does not
choices.you: You announced Madrid would fall within days.
choices.r: Your announcement is broadcast to the world. Foreign journalists start packing for Madrid.

choices.t: Say nothing until the city has fallen
choices.r: Your silence unnerves Madrid's defenders more than any boast.

plans.title: Casa de Campo · 7 November 1936
plans.text: One of your tanks is knocked out in the Casa de Campo. On the body of an officer inside, the Republicans find your complete plan of attack.

ledger.hist: On 7 November the Republicans found the Nationalist attack plan in a disabled tank and moved their reserves to meet it.

choices.r: Your staff work through the night. The attack goes in two days late.

choices.t: Keep to the plan: there is no time
choices.h: The enemy will know where you strike first
choices.r: The columns go forward as ordered.

brigades.title: Madrid · 8 November 1936
brigades.text: The XI International Brigade marches down the Gran Vía to cheering crowds: volunteers from France, Germany, Britain, Poland and beyond. Soviet fighters appear over the city for the first time.

choices.t: Call them foreign communists in your broadcasts
choices.r: Your broadcasts speak of a Red invasion of Spain.

choices.t: Ask Berlin and Rome for more aircraft, now
choices.r: More aircraft are promised for the coming days.

recognition.title: Salamanca · 18 November 1936
recognition.text: Germany and Italy formally recognise your government. Berlin is forming a full air unit for Spain, with its own commanders: the Condor Legion.

ledger.hist: Germany and Italy recognised Franco's government on 18 November 1936. The Condor Legion arrived that month. In April 1937 it destroyed Guernica.

choices.t: Accept the Condor Legion under German command
choices.you: You accepted the Condor Legion under German command.
choices.r: The Legion's commander answers to Berlin, not to you.

choices.t: Insist it serves under your officers
choices.r: Berlin agrees on paper. In practice the Germans do as they please.

joseAntonioDeath.title: Alicante · 20 November 1936
joseAntonioDeath.text: News comes from Alicante: José Antonio Primo de Rivera has been tried and shot by the Republic. The Falange has lost its founder.

choices.t: Make him the martyr of the movement
choices.r: His name is painted on church walls across the Nationalist zone, next to yours.
The Falangists notice how little you say.

jaAlive.title: Salamanca · 20 November 1936
jaAlive.text: José Antonio is alive and free in your zone, and the Falange's young men look to him, not to you. He wants the movement to stay independent of the army.

choices.t: Give him a ministry and keep him close
choices.r: José Antonio joins your government and argues with you at every meeting.
The Falange splits between his followers and yours.

massArmy.title: Salamanca · 1 December 1936
massArmy.text: Your columns are worn out after Madrid. To finish the war you need a real army: conscripts from the provinces you hold, more Moroccan recruits, and the troops Mussolini is offering.

ledger.hist: Through 1937 the Nationalists conscripted hundreds of thousands of Spaniards and recruited tens of thousands of Moroccans. About 50,000 Italian troops were serving in Spain by early 1937.

choices.you: You called up the conscript classes.
choices.r: Recruiting offices open in every town you hold. Young men from Galicia, Castile and Navarre are drafted and sent to training camps.
Recruiters fan out through the Rif, where drought and hunger make the army's pay hard to refuse.
Thousands of Italian "volunteers" land at Cádiz under their own generals. Their commanders answer to Rome.

malaga.title: Málaga · 8 February 1937
malaga.text: Queipo's columns and the Italian Corps have taken Málaga in a few days. Tens of thousands of people are fleeing east along the coast road to Almería. Your warships and aircraft can see the road from the sea.

ledger.hist: Málaga fell on 8 February 1937. Refugees fleeing to Almería were shelled from the sea and bombed from the air, and thousands died on the road. Thousands more were executed in Málaga in the months that followed.

choices.t: Order the road shelled and bombed
choices.you: You had the coast road attacked.
choices.r: For days the cruisers and aircraft attack the road. A Canadian doctor, Norman Bethune, drives the wounded to Almería and tells the world what he saw.
Your ships hold their fire. The refugees reach Almería exhausted, and some of the militiamen among them will fight again.

choices.t: Let Queipo run Málaga as he sees fit
choices.you: You gave Queipo a free hand in Málaga.
choices.r: Queipo's courts-martial work through the prisons of Málaga for months.

turnNorth.title: Salamanca · 23 March 1937
turnNorth.text: Madrid has beaten off every attempt to take or surround it. In the north, the Basque Country, Santander and Asturias are cut off from the rest of the Republic, with the iron mines, steelworks and arms factories you need. Your German advisers urge you to turn north.

ledger.hist: After Guadalajara, Franco gave up trying to take Madrid and turned against the isolated Republican north. The capital held out until March 1939.

choices.r: Mola will command the offensive. The Condor Legion moves its aircraft to the airfields around Vitoria.

choices.t: Try for Madrid one more time
choices.h: A long shot · costly if it fails

win.r: Your attack from the north-west finds the defenders exhausted. Madrid's government flees and the city surrenders. The war goes on, but it will be shorter.

lose.r: The attack breaks against the same trenches as before. Two weeks and thousands of men are gone, and the north is still waiting.

durango.title: Vitoria · 31 March 1937
durango.text: Mola opens the northern offensive with a warning to the Basques: "If submission is not immediate, I will raze all Vizcaya to the ground, beginning with the industries of war." This morning Italian and German aircraft bombed the market town of Durango. The Condor Legion's chief of staff, Wolfram von Richthofen, wants a free hand to do the same wherever it helps the advance.

ledger.k: The air war in the north
ledger.hist: Mola's offensive began on 31 March 1937 with the bombing of Durango, which killed more than 250 people. Franco's headquarters backed the Condor Legion's raids in support of the advance.

choices.t: Give the Condor Legion a free hand
choices.you: You gave the Condor Legion a free hand.
choices.r: Richthofen's bombers will hit roads, bridges and towns behind the Basque lines as he sees fit.

choices.t: Bomb only the front line and the factories
choices.you: You limited the bombing to military targets.
choices.r: Richthofen complains to Berlin that he is fighting with one hand tied.

choices.you: You left the air war to Mola.
choices.r: Mola's staff and the Legion plan the raids together. You will be told afterwards.

unification.title: Salamanca · 19 April 1937
unification.text: Your brother-in-law, Ramón Serrano Súñer, has a plan. The Falange and the Carlists have tens of thousands of armed volunteers and quarrel constantly. Merge them by decree into one party, with you as its leader, and nobody will be able to organise against you.

ledger.hist: On 19 April 1937 Franco merged the Falange and the Carlists into one party, FET y de las JONS, with himself as its leader. It remained the only legal party in Spain until 1977.

choices.t: Decree the merger and lead the new party
choices.you: You merged the parties and led them yourself.
choices.r: The decree creates the Falange Española Tradicionalista y de las JONS. Its leader is you.

choices.t: Leave the parties as they are
choices.h: No new power · no new rivals
choices.r: Falangists and Carlists keep their own militias, newspapers and quarrels.

choices.t: Put the Falange's leader, Manuel Hedilla, in charge
choices.you: You gave the united party to Hedilla.
choices.r: Hedilla, a former ship's mechanic admired in Berlin, takes over the united party, and its militias answer to him.

hedilla.title: Salamanca · 25 April 1937
hedilla.text: Manuel Hedilla, the Falange's leader, refuses the seat you offered him on the new party's council and tells his followers to take orders only from him. Your police arrest him, and a court-martial sentences him to death.

ledger.hist: Hedilla was sentenced to death for resisting the merger. Franco commuted the sentence and Hedilla spent four years in prison.

choices.r: Hedilla goes to prison in the Canary Islands. The Falange learns who is in charge.

choices.h: Terror · the Falange is cowed · Germany shocked
choices.r: Hedilla is shot. No Falangist will defy you openly again.

choices.h: The Falange is grateful · you look weak
choices.r: Hedilla walks free and tells everyone that you backed down.

bilbaoFalls.title: Bilbao · 19 June 1937
bilbaoFalls.text: Bilbao falls. The Basque army retreats west toward Santander, leaving behind the blast furnaces, shipyards and arms factories that its leaders refused to blow up. Basque officials ask what will become of their self-government and their language.

ledger.hist: Bilbao fell on 19 June 1937 with its industry intact. Franco abolished the economic self-government of Vizcaya and Guipúzcoa as "traitor provinces", and Basque iron ore helped pay Germany for its aid.

choices.t: Abolish Basque self-government and ban the language
choices.r: Your decree calls Vizcaya and Guipúzcoa "traitor provinces" and strips them of their old rights. Basque is banned from schools and public life.

choices.t: Leave the provinces their old rights
choices.you: You left the Basques their old rights.
choices.r: Navarre and Álava kept their rights for siding with you. Now Vizcaya and Guipúzcoa keep theirs too, and your hardliners say you are rewarding treason.

choices.t: Ship the iron ore to Germany to pay for arms
choices.you: You sent Basque ore to Germany.
choices.r: Within weeks, ore ships sail from Bilbao for Hamburg and German shells come back the other way.

bishops.title: Salamanca · 1 July 1937
bishops.text: Abroad, Guernica and the executions behind your lines have turned many Catholics against you. Cardinal Gomá offers to answer with a letter from the Spanish bishops to the bishops of the world, explaining why the Church stands with your side.

ledger.hist: On 1 July 1937 the Spanish bishops published a collective letter supporting Franco's side. The Bishop of Vitoria and the Cardinal of Tarragona refused to sign.

choices.you: You asked the bishops to write.
choices.r: The letter calls the war a crusade and is read out in churches from Dublin to Buenos Aires. Two bishops refuse to sign it.

choices.t: Keep the Church out of it
choices.h: Legitimacy falls a little · the army approves
choices.you: You kept the Church out of it.
choices.r: Gomá is disappointed. Your officers say wars are won by soldiers, not bishops.

santona.title: Santoña · 26 August 1937
santona.text: Cut off on the coast at Santoña, some 20,000 Basque soldiers have surrendered to the Italians, not to you. The Italian commanders promised them their lives, and ships to take their officers and politicians abroad. They are already boarding.

ledger.hist: Franco refused to honour the Italian agreement at Santoña. The Basque soldiers were taken off the ships and imprisoned, and many faced courts-martial.

choices.t: Repudiate the pact. Take them off the ships
choices.h: The historical choice · terror · Italy offended
choices.r: Your troops march the prisoners off the ships. Many will face courts-martial. The Italian officers who gave their word are humiliated.
The ships sail. Rome is grateful, and foreign newspapers report that you kept an ally's word.

choices.t: Let the soldiers go home and try the officers
choices.you: You released the soldiers and tried the officers.
choices.r: Thousands of Basque conscripts walk home. Their officers are taken to prison.

northFalls.title: Gijón · 21 October 1937
northFalls.text: The war in the north is over. You hold the coal of Asturias, the iron and steel of Bilbao, and tens of thousands of prisoners. Your own factories can now arm your army.

ledger.hist: The fall of the north in October 1937 gave Franco its mines and heavy industry. Tens of thousands of prisoners were put to forced labour.

choices.t: Put the prisoners to work in labour battalions
choices.you: You put the prisoners to forced labour.
choices.r: Prisoners are sent to rebuild roads and bridges and to work in the mines, under armed guard.

choices.t: Draft the young prisoners into your army
choices.r: Asturian miners are handed uniforms and rifles. Your officers watch them closely.

choices.t: Release those accused of no crime
choices.you: You released prisoners accused of no crime.
choices.r: Thousands go home to their villages, where the local Falange keeps a list of their names.

cold.title: Teruel · 8 January 1938
cold.text: Teruel's last defenders have surrendered to the Republic. The temperature has fallen to twenty degrees below zero. Lorries freeze on the roads, and you are losing more men to frostbite than to bullets.

ledger.hist: Teruel was fought in one of the coldest winters in memory, at around −20 °C. Thousands of soldiers on both sides suffered frostbite.

choices.t: Requisition winter clothing and fuel at any cost
choices.r: Lorries of greatcoats and blankets crawl up from Zaragoza. Your men curse the cold, but most of them keep their toes.

choices.you: You pressed on through the cold.
choices.r: The columns move on, leaving a trail of men too frozen to walk.

choices.t: Wait for the weather to break
choices.h: 10 days lost · the Republic digs in
choices.r: The blizzards pass after ten days. The Republic has used them to fortify the ruins.

firstGovernment.title: Burgos · 30 January 1938
firstGovernment.text: You form your first real government, to replace the committee of officials that has run your zone since 1936. The generals, the Falange, the monarchists and the Church all want their men in it.

ledger.hist: Franco formed his first government on 30 January 1938, balancing generals, Falangists, monarchists and Catholics. He chaired the cabinet himself until 1973.

choices.t: Balance them all, and keep the army for yourself
choices.r: Generals, Falangists, monarchists and Catholics share the ministries, and none of them can rule without you. Serrano Súñer takes the Interior.

choices.t: Give the Falange the key ministries
choices.r: Blue shirts fill the ministries. Kindelán and the monarchists stop coming to dinner.

choices.you: You filled the government with generals.
choices.r: Your cabinet meetings look like a staff conference.

barcelonaBombing.title: Barcelona · 16 March 1938
barcelonaBombing.text: On Mussolini's own orders, Italian bombers from Mallorca are attacking Barcelona every few hours, day and night, to break its people's will. Nobody consulted you. The bombs are falling on the city centre and the foreign press is reporting hundreds dead.

ledger.hist: Italian bombers attacked Barcelona from 16 to 18 March 1938, killing nearly a thousand people. Franco, who had not been consulted, asked for the raids to stop.

choices.h: The historical choice · legitimacy · Italy cools
choices.r: After three days the raids stop. Nearly a thousand people have been killed.
The raids go on until Rome decides they have made their point.
Your praise is printed in Rome and quoted with disgust in London and Washington.

xyz.title: Castellón · 5 July 1938
xyz.text: Your drive on Valencia has run into the XYZ Line: belts of trenches and bunkers dug into the mountains north of the city. Your divisions are losing thousands of men a week for a few kilometres of rock.

ledger.hist: In July 1938 the Nationalist advance on Valencia was stopped at the XYZ Line, with heavy losses.

choices.r: The attacks go on through the July heat. The line bends but does not break.

choices.h: Morale · Valencia is safe for now
choices.r: Your divisions dig in and wait for fresh troops and shells.

choices.t: Bomb Valencia's port to cut its supplies
choices.you: You bombed the port of Valencia.
choices.r: Italian bombers hit the harbour. British merchant ships are among those sunk, and London protests.

brigadesLeave.title: Burgos · 28 October 1938
brigadesLeave.text: The Republic has sent the International Brigades home, hoping the League of Nations will make Germany and Italy withdraw too. Today the volunteers paraded through Barcelona for the last time, and Dolores Ibárruri told them: "You can go proudly. You are history." Britain asks you to send some of your Italians home in return.

ledger.hist: About 35,000 volunteers from more than 50 countries served in the International Brigades. They paraded through Barcelona for the last time on 28 October 1938. Franco sent about 10,000 Italians home that month.

choices.h: The historical choice · legitimacy · Italy cools
choices.r: Ten thousand Italian veterans sail home from Cádiz. London puts its new agreement with Rome into force.
Britain's ambassador notes your answer without comment.

ebroEnds.title: The Ebro · 16 November 1938
ebroEnds.text: The last Republican troops cross back over the Ebro and blow up the bridges behind them. Of the army that crossed in July, little is left. Catalonia lies open.

ledger.hist: The Battle of the Ebro ended on 16 November 1938. Franco attacked Catalonia five weeks later, after Germany sent new weapons in exchange for mining rights.

choices.r: Your exhausted divisions are pulled out of the line for the first time since July.
Tired men are marched straight back toward the front.

christmas.title: Lleida · 23 December 1938
christmas.text: Pope Pius XI has asked both sides to stop fighting over Christmas. Your army is ready on the Segre river with 300,000 men, new German guns and hundreds of aircraft. The Republic's army in Catalonia has barely recovered from the Ebro.

ledger.hist: Franco rejected the Pope's call for a Christmas truce and attacked Catalonia on 23 December 1938.

choices.r: Your guns open fire at dawn.

choices.you: You agreed to a Christmas truce.
choices.r: For a week the guns are quiet along the Segre. Both sides use it to bring up shells.

choices.t: Bomb the Republic's roads and railways first
choices.you: You bombed the roads and railways first.
choices.r: The Condor Legion pounds the junctions behind the Republican line for two days before you attack.

barcelonaFalls.title: Barcelona · 26 January 1939
barcelonaFalls.text: Barcelona falls almost without a fight. The Republic's government has fled north toward the French border. Your troops march down the Diagonal while some crowds cheer and other people stay behind closed shutters.

ledger.hist: Barcelona fell on 26 January 1939. The new authorities banned the public use of Catalan and began a wave of arrests and executions.

choices.t: Hold a victory mass in the cathedral
choices.r: The cathedral is packed with officers and priests.

choices.t: Ban Catalan from public life and purge the city
choices.you: You banned Catalan and purged the city.
choices.r: Catalan is banned in schools, newspapers and public offices. The new authorities begin collecting denunciations.

choices.t: Send in food, not just soldiers
choices.r: Lorries of bread follow your troops, and soup kitchens open on the Ramblas.

retirada.title: Figueres · 5 February 1939
retirada.text: Half a million people are walking toward the French border through the snow: soldiers, officials and families carrying what they can. The Republic's president, Manuel Azaña, crosses on foot. France is letting the civilians in and penning the soldiers behind barbed wire on the beaches.

ledger.hist: About 450,000 people fled into France in January and February 1939. Many were held for months in camps on the beaches. Tens of thousands never returned, and thousands later died in Nazi camps.

choices.t: Let them go. Spain is better off without them
choices.r: Some will come back in the months ahead and face your courts. Many will never see Spain again.

choices.t: Promise that those with no blood on their hands may return
choices.you: You promised a safe return to those accused of no crime.
choices.r: Thousands turn back at the border. Your own courts will decide whether your promise means anything.

choices.t: Bomb the roads to the border
choices.you: You bombed the roads to the border.
choices.r: Your aircraft attack the columns on the roads near Figueres. Photographs of the dead reach every newspaper in France.

responsibilities.title: Burgos · 9 February 1939
responsibilities.text: Your jurists have drafted a Law of Political Responsibilities. It will punish anyone who supported the Republic since October 1934, even where no crime under the old law was committed: fines, confiscations, prison, banishment from their home towns.

ledger.hist: The Law of Political Responsibilities of 9 February 1939 made support for the Republic since October 1934 a punishable offence. Hundreds of thousands of people were investigated under it.

choices.r: The law takes effect at once. Special courts will hear hundreds of thousands of cases.

choices.t: Sign it, but only for those accused of crimes
choices.you: You limited the law to crimes.
choices.r: The courts will still be busy, but a membership card is no longer enough to convict.

choices.h: Legitimacy · the army and the Falange are furious
choices.r: Your generals and the Falange are stunned. Queipo says on the radio that you have gone soft.

recognition39.title: Burgos · 27 February 1939
recognition39.text: Britain and France recognise your government as the government of Spain. The Republic's president, Manuel Azaña, resigns in France. Only the Republic's last zone in the centre and south-east still holds out.

ledger.hist: Britain and France recognised Franco's government on 27 February 1939, without any binding guarantee against reprisals.

choices.t: Promise London there will be no reprisals
choices.h: Legitimacy · a promise you may not keep
choices.r: The British ambassador sends your promise to London. Your courts carry on.
Your answer is that Spain's justice is Spain's business.

madridEnters.title: Madrid · 28 March 1939
madridEnters.text: Your troops enter Madrid. The city that held out for two and a half years surrenders without a shot. In the ports of the south-east, thousands of people wait on the quays for ships that mostly never come.

ledger.hist: Nationalist troops entered Madrid on 28 March 1939. At Alicante, about 15,000 Republicans waited for ships; most were captured by Italian troops on 31 March.

choices.t: Let the Italians take the port of Alicante
choices.r: Italian troops reach Alicante on 31 March. The people on the quays are marched off to camps.

choices.t: Let foreign ships take the refugees
choices.you: You let foreign ships evacuate the refugees.
choices.r: British and French ships take thousands off the harbour wall at Alicante.

valenciaEnd.title: Madrid · 28 March 1939
valenciaEnd.text: Madrid has been yours for two years. Now Valencia and the last towns of the south-east surrender one after another. In the ports, thousands of people wait on the quays for ships that mostly never come.

ledger.hist: At Alicante, about 15,000 Republicans waited for ships at the end of March 1939; most were captured by Italian troops on 31 March.

choices.r: Italian troops reach Alicante on 31 March. The people on the quays are marched off to camps.

choices.t: Let foreign ships take the refugees
choices.you: You let foreign ships evacuate the refugees.
choices.r: British and French ships take thousands off the harbour wall at Alicante.

lastReport.title: Burgos · 1 April 1939
lastReport.text: In bed with influenza, you correct the last war report in your own hand: "Today, with the Red Army captive and disarmed, the Nationalist troops have reached their final military objectives. The war is over."

choices.t: Call it a crusade, and the victory yours
choices.r: Your victory will be celebrated every year with a parade. The defeated will not be allowed to mourn their dead.

choices.t: Call it the end of a war between Spaniards
choices.r: Your words are printed in every newspaper. What happens next will matter more.

deck.title: Engine trouble
deck.text: Over the sea, the Dragon Rapide's port engine starts to cough. Captain Bebb shouts over the noise that he can probably keep going.

choices.t: Land at the nearest strip and repair it
choices.r: Mechanics at a French airstrip fix a fuel line. You hear on the radio that the rising has begun without you.

win.r: The engine clears its throat and settles. Nobody mentions it again.

lose.r: The engine dies over the coast. Bebb puts down in a field, and it takes a day to get moving again.

deck.title: The tourists
deck.text: The plane was hired in London with a retired British major and two young women aboard, posing as holidaymakers. Major Pollard wants to know how long this charade must go on.

choices.t: Pay them well and send them home
choices.r: The major pockets the money and promises never to speak of it. He speaks of it for the rest of his life.

choices.t: Ask them to keep up the act as far as Casablanca

win.r: French officials wave the English tourists and their quiet friend straight through.

lose.r: A French official finds the story absurd and keeps you all waiting until evening.

deck.title: A telegram from Mola
deck.text: Mola asks you to confirm that you will lead the Army of Africa under his plan for the rising.

choices.t: Reply warmly. You serve the rising
choices.r: Mola is reassured. He begins to treat you as a dependable subordinate.

choices.t: Reply as an equal, not a subordinate
choices.r: Your reply is polite and gives nothing away. Mola reads it as a warning.

deck.title: Customs at Casablanca
deck.text: A French customs officer studies your diplomatic passport, then your face. You shaved off your moustache this morning.

win.r: He shrugs and stamps the passport.

lose.r: He calls his superior. It takes until evening to sort out, and someone takes a photograph.

choices.r: The envelope disappears. So does his interest.

deck.title: Bad news on the radio
deck.text: Radio reports say the rising has failed in Madrid and Barcelona. The officers around you go quiet.

choices.t: Tell them the rising will win
choices.r: Your calm spreads. Nobody asks how you can be so sure.

choices.t: Admit it may be a long war
choices.r: Your frankness unsettles them, but word gets around that you see clearly.

deck.title: Juan March's credit
deck.text: The financier Juan March, the richest man in Spain, offers you credit for aircraft, fuel and pay.

choices.r: The money arrives through London banks. March will expect favours later.

choices.t: Decline. You will owe no one
choices.r: March is surprised and a little offended. He will offer again, to someone else.

deck.title: The fleet
deck.text: Republican warships ride at anchor in the Strait. Their crews turned on their officers when they refused to support the Republic, and elected committees now command them.

choices.t: Send the Italian bombers against the fleet

win.r: Bombs straddle the destroyers. Their captains grow cautious and keep further out.

lose.r: The bombers miss, and the ships move out of range.

choices.t: Leave the fleet alone for now
choices.r: The warships keep patrolling.

deck.title: Mola's envoys in Berlin
deck.text: Mola has sent his own men to Germany to ask for aircraft. If Berlin deals with both of you, it can play you off against each other.

choices.t: Insist that all German aid comes through you
choices.r: Berlin agrees to deal with you alone. Mola learns of it from the Germans.

choices.t: Agree to share the channel with Mola
choices.r: Mola appreciates the gesture. Some of the aid will go north.

deck.title: Tangier
deck.text: Republican warships refuel in the international port of Tangier, under the protection of the city's foreign administration.

choices.r: The commission promises to look into it. Diplomats notice that you used the proper channels.
Rome approves. London does not.

deck.title: Recruiting in the Rif
deck.text: Your officers propose recruiting thousands more Moroccan Regulares from the Rif, with pay in advance and promises to local leaders.

choices.r: Three thousand men sign on in a week.

choices.h: Fewer men · a promise to keep
choices.r: Fifteen hundred men sign on. Their leaders will remember what you promised.
Your officers shrug and get back to work.

deck.title: Fuel for the Junkers
deck.text: The transport aircraft burn fuel faster than Tetuán can supply it. A Shell agent in Tangier will sell more, at a high price.

choices.r: The fuel arrives by lorry at night.
Fewer flights will cross each day.

deck.title: A foreign journalist
deck.text: An American reporter asks for an interview about your aims in this war.

win.r: The article calls you calm and professional.

lose.r: You say you will save Spain from Marxism at any cost. He asks whether that means shooting half of Spain, and you do not say no. The quote travels.

choices.r: He writes about the general who would not talk.

deck.title: Lost bombers
deck.text: Of the twelve Italian bombers sent to you, three never arrive. One crashed into the sea and two landed in French territory, where officials are asking awkward questions.

choices.r: Rome sends replacements, and an invoice.
Nine bombers will have to do.

deck.title: The Khalifa of Tetuán
deck.text: The Khalifa, the nominal ruler of the Spanish zone of Morocco, offers his public blessing for the rising if you respect Moroccan religious life.

choices.r: The ceremony brings a thousand more volunteers.
The Khalifa is courteous and unconvinced.

deck.title: Heat on the road
deck.text: It is August in Extremadura. Water is short and men collapse on the march.

choices.r: The column keeps its pace and leaves stragglers behind.

choices.t: Rest during the day, march at night
choices.r: The men recover. The column loses a day.

deck.title: The ammunition train
deck.text: A train from Sevilla brings ammunition. Queipo de Llano makes sure everyone knows who sent it.

choices.r: Queipo reads your thanks aloud on Radio Sevilla.
Queipo notices the silence.

deck.title: Ambush in the olive groves
deck.text: Militiamen open fire from the olive groves along the road.

choices.r: The column clears the groves at a cost.
The detour takes two days through dry hills.

deck.title: German pilots
deck.text: German airmen flying your Ju 52s offer to bomb Republican positions ahead of your columns, and Madrid itself.

choices.t: Approve raids on the front only
choices.r: The bombers hit militia trenches ahead of the column.
Bombs fall on Madrid. Photographs of the damage appear in foreign newspapers.
The Germans grumble and keep flying.

deck.title: Prisoners on the road
deck.text: Your column has taken several hundred prisoners. Guarding them slows the advance.

choices.t: Send them back to Sevilla under guard
choices.r: Two hundred of your men march them south.

choices.t: Hand them over to the local Falange
choices.r: The column moves on. What happens to them is not recorded in your reports.

deck.title: A bishop's blessing
deck.text: The bishop of a captured town offers to bless your troops in public and to call the war a crusade.

choices.r: The ceremony is photographed for every newspaper in rebel Spain.
The bishop blesses the column as it passes.

deck.title: Deserters
deck.text: Conscripts from Sevilla are slipping away at night.

choices.t: Make an example of the ringleaders
choices.r: The desertions stop.
The desertions slow.
Four hundred men are gone by the end of the week.

deck.title: Help from Portugal
deck.text: Salazar's government in Portugal lets supplies cross the border and hands Republican refugees back to you.

choices.r: Lorries cross the border at night.
London protests to Lisbon. Rome approves.

deck.title: Carlist volunteers
deck.text: The Carlists of Navarre offer volunteer battalions, the requetés. Their leaders want a voice in any future government.

choices.r: Fifteen hundred men in red berets join your columns.
The Carlists go north to fight under Mola instead.

deck.title: Sickness in the column
deck.text: Typhoid has broken out in two companies.

choices.r: The outbreak is contained.
The sickness spreads through the column.

deck.title: Yagüe complains
deck.text: Yagüe says your orders are too cautious. He is popular with the legionnaires.

choices.r: Yagüe salutes stiffly.

choices.t: Praise him in the next communiqué
choices.r: The legionnaires cheer when the communiqué is read out.

deck.title: Radio Sevilla
deck.text: Every night Queipo fills Radio Sevilla with boasts, jokes and threats. Listeners across Spain know his voice better than yours.

choices.r: Your broadcasts are drier than Queipo's, but they are yours.
Queipo keeps talking.

deck.title: The monarchists
deck.text: Monarchist officers ask you to promise that the king will return once the war is won.

choices.r: Kindelán shakes your hand for a long time.
You say the army must decide nothing until the war is won.

deck.title: Buying mules
deck.text: Your lorries cannot reach every hill. Local dealers offer mules at wartime prices.

choices.r: Supplies reach the forward companies.
The men carry what they can.

deck.title: The foreign press
deck.text: Newspapers in London, Paris and New York report killings behind your lines.

choices.t: Invite correspondents to see for themselves
choices.r: The correspondents see what you show them, and some of what you do not.

choices.t: Ban foreign reporters from the front
choices.r: The reporters write about the ban instead.

choices.t: Blame the reports on Red propaganda
choices.r: Your supporters believe you. Few others do.

deck.title: The German crews
deck.text: The Lufthansa pilots flying your Ju 52s are civilians on loan. They want danger money, paid in pesetas, before they fly another day.

choices.r: The pilots fly double shifts all week.

choices.t: Tell them to take it up with Berlin
choices.r: Berlin pays them in the end, and remembers who did not.

deck.title: British warships at Gibraltar
deck.text: Royal Navy ships watch the Strait from Gibraltar. Britain says it is neutral, but your aircraft keep flying close to its harbour.

choices.t: Assure London you will respect Gibraltar
choices.r: The British consul in Tetuán calls you a reasonable man.
The British keep watching.

deck.title: Non-intervention
deck.text: Britain and France propose that no country send arms to Spain. Germany and Italy sign the agreement and keep sending aircraft anyway. The Republic, which can no longer buy French weapons, is furious.

choices.r: You call it a wise step toward peace, knowing it hurts only your enemy.

choices.t: Denounce it as a plot against Spain
choices.r: Rome applauds. London sighs.

deck.title: Portuguese volunteers
deck.text: Several hundred Portuguese volunteers, the Viriatos, cross the border to join your columns.

choices.r: The Legion has always taken foreigners.
Lisbon is quietly relieved.

deck.title: The harvest
deck.text: Villages along the road have just brought in the wheat harvest. Your quartermasters want it.

choices.r: The granaries are emptied. The villages will go hungry this winter.
Some farmers cheer the column as it passes.

deck.title: The hospitals of Sevilla
deck.text: The hospitals in Sevilla are full of your wounded, short of bandages, morphine and surgeons.

choices.t: Divert supplies and money to them
choices.r: Word gets back to the front that the wounded are cared for.
The men notice.

deck.title: A German observer
deck.text: Lieutenant Colonel Walter Warlimont arrives from Berlin to report on how German aid is being used. He wants to see the front for himself.

choices.r: Warlimont's report to Berlin is glowing.
Warlimont writes that you are secretive.

deck.title: Irún falls
deck.text: Mola's troops have taken Irún and closed the French border to the Basques. The newspapers are full of Mola.

choices.r: Mola thanks you. The press calls you both heroes.

choices.t: Point out it was your German bombers
choices.r: Officers in Burgos repeat it. Mola hears it from three of them.

deck.title: Back pay
deck.text: The Moroccan Regulares have not been paid for six weeks. Their officers warn of trouble.

choices.r: The arrears are paid in silver duros.
The promise is received in silence.

deck.title: A chaplain's letter
deck.text: An army chaplain writes to you directly. He has heard confessions from men about to be shot, and asks you to stop the executions behind the lines.

choices.t: Order the executions restricted to court-martial cases
choices.r: Some local commanders obey. Queipo calls the order an insult.
The letter goes into a drawer.

deck.title: A captured aviator
deck.text: Your men have captured a Republican pilot whose plane came down near the road.

choices.t: Offer him for exchange through the Red Cross
choices.r: The Red Cross arranges an exchange for one of your officers.

choices.t: Hand him to the military court
choices.r: His trial takes twenty minutes.

deck.title: Your brother Nicolás
deck.text: Your staff is overwhelmed by politics: monarchists, Falangists, Carlists, bishops and foreign envoys. Your brother Nicolás offers to run your political office.

choices.r: Nicolás starts working the telephones. Within a week every faction has his number.

choices.t: Keep politics in the army's hands
choices.r: The army keeps the files, and loses some of them.

deck.title: Bombing Madrid
deck.text: German and Italian aircrews propose bombing Madrid itself, to break the city's will before your columns arrive.

choices.r: Bombs fall on the Puerta del Sol and the working-class districts. Photographs of dead children appear in newspapers abroad.
The aircrews grumble about wasted fuel.

deck.title: The fifth column
deck.text: General Mola tells journalists that four columns are marching on Madrid, and a fifth column of supporters inside the city will rise to meet them. In Madrid, thousands of suspects are arrested.

choices.t: Repeat the claim on the radio
choices.r: The phrase "fifth column" spreads around the world.

choices.t: Order silence about agents in the city
choices.r: Mola is annoyed to be told to keep quiet.

deck.title: Spain's gold
deck.text: Your agents report that the Republic has shipped most of the Bank of Spain's gold reserves to Moscow, to pay for Soviet weapons.

choices.r: Your press office calls it the theft of the century.

choices.t: Use it to press the banks for credit
choices.r: Bankers in London decide your side is the safer bet.

deck.title: Winter on the plateau
deck.text: Nights around Madrid are already freezing. Many of your Moroccan troops still wear summer uniforms.

choices.r: The coats arrive before the first snow.

choices.t: They will be in Madrid's barracks soon
choices.r: Men fall sick in the trenches.

deck.title: Italian volunteers
deck.text: Rome offers to send 'volunteers': in truth, whole divisions of the Italian army with their own commanders.

choices.r: The first Italian ships sail for Cádiz.
Rome sends machines, and a little wounded pride.
Mussolini takes it personally.

deck.title: Reports from the villages
deck.text: Republican radio describes looting and rape by your troops in the villages around Madrid. Foreign reporters are asking questions.

choices.t: Issue strict orders on discipline and enforce them
choices.r: A few men are court-martialled. The reports become rarer.
Fear runs ahead of your columns.

deck.title: A journalist in Málaga
deck.text: Your police have arrested Arthur Koestler, a Hungarian writer working for a London newspaper, at a house outside Málaga. He is accused of spying for the Republic, and a court-martial is ready to sentence him to death.

choices.h: Terror · the foreign press turns on you
choices.r: The British press campaigns for him daily. Every story mentions the death cell in Sevilla.

choices.t: Exchange him for one of your own prisoners
choices.r: After months in prison, Koestler is swapped for the wife of one of your pilots, held by the Republic. He will write a book about his cell.
Koestler is put on a boat at Gibraltar with a warning never to return.

deck.title: The German ambassador
deck.text: Germany's ambassador, General Wilhelm Faupel, lectures you on how to run your war and your politics. He spends his evenings with the Falange's leaders and tells Berlin that you are slow and unimaginative.

choices.r: By the summer Faupel is gone, replaced by a diplomat who knows his place.

choices.h: Germany warms · the Falange grows bolder
choices.r: Faupel reports to Berlin that you are finally listening.

deck.title: The Italian general
deck.text: General Mario Roatta, commander of the Italian Corps, wants his divisions to fight together under his own orders, not scattered among your columns. Mussolini wants a victory he can call Italian.

choices.r: Roatta gets a sector north-east of Madrid, toward Guadalajara.

choices.t: Keep the Italians under Spanish command
choices.r: Roatta complains to Rome. Rome complains to you.

deck.title: Winter in the trenches
deck.text: Around Madrid both armies have dug in for the winter in the Casa de Campo and University City. In places the trenches are close enough to shout across, and your officers report men trading cigarettes with the enemy.

choices.r: Two sergeants are court-martialled, and the shouting stops.
Cigarette papers from your side are swapped for tobacco from theirs.
Promises of white bread and safe conduct bring a trickle of deserters across the lines.

deck.title: The children's ship
deck.text: The Basque government is evacuating children from Bilbao. The liner Habana is about to sail for England with nearly four thousand of them, escorted by the Royal Navy. Your blockade ships are watching.

choices.r: The Habana reaches Southampton. Most of the children will be sent home within a few years; some never return.

choices.t: Protest that they will be taught to hate Spain
choices.r: Your press calls it a kidnapping. The children sail anyway.

deck.title: Blockade runners
deck.text: British merchant ships are running your blockade of Bilbao with food. Your cruiser Almirante Cervera could stop them, but British warships are escorting them to the edge of Spanish waters.

choices.r: The British captains turn back once, then come again with their navy in sight.
Mines are laid off the estuary. One merchant ship is damaged and the rest wait offshore.
Bilbao eats for another month.

deck.title: The Navarrese brigades
deck.text: The Carlist volunteers of Navarre are your best mountain troops, and their red berets are everywhere in the hills of Biscay. Their leaders want a promise: after the war, Navarre keeps its old self-government.

choices.r: Navarre will keep its ancient rights. The requetés go back up the hills singing.
The Carlist leaders leave your office unhappy, but they fight on.

deck.title: New fighters
deck.text: The Condor Legion is receiving Germany's newest fighter, the Messerschmitt Bf 109, to test it against Soviet aircraft. Its commanders want the best airfields and first call on fuel.

choices.r: The new fighters sweep the Soviet Polikarpovs from the northern skies.

choices.t: Keep the fuel for your own lorries
choices.r: The Germans grumble and test their aircraft anyway.

deck.title: The Irish Brigade
deck.text: Eoin O'Duffy's Irish Brigade, seven hundred volunteers who came to fight for Catholic Spain, has seen little action and less glory. Its men are quarrelling and want to go home.

choices.r: They sail from Lisbon in June. O'Duffy writes a book about their crusade.

choices.t: Put them back in the line
choices.r: The Irish go back to the Jarama trenches, sullen and few.

deck.title: The Labour Charter
deck.text: Your ministers present a Labour Charter, the Fuero del Trabajo. The Falange wants it to read like a revolution, the Church like a sermon, and the employers like a guarantee that the unions are gone for good.

choices.r: The Charter promises work, bread and justice under a single state-run union.
The Charter quotes the papal encyclicals and promises a family wage.
Strikes become a crime against the nation. Factory owners send you warm telegrams.

deck.title: Negrín's Thirteen Points
deck.text: The Republic's prime minister, Juan Negrín, has published thirteen points for peace: Spanish independence, the withdrawal of foreign troops, a vote on the form of government, and an amnesty for both sides.

choices.r: Your answer is that there can be no peace with the Reds, only surrender.

choices.t: Let the Vatican sound them out quietly
choices.r: Messages pass back and forth through Rome for a few weeks, and nothing comes of it.

deck.title: Yagüe's speech
deck.text: At a Falange dinner in Burgos, General Yagüe, your old column commander, praised the courage of the Republic's soldiers, demanded the release of political prisoners, and mocked the Germans and Italians. The embassies want to know whether he speaks for you.

choices.t: Relieve him of his command for a while
choices.r: Yagüe spends a few weeks without a command, then returns to the front chastened.
Yagüe's words are repeated in every officers' mess.

deck.title: The cavalry at the Alfambra
deck.text: On the frozen plain of the Alfambra, north of Teruel, General Monasterio has a cavalry division of several thousand horsemen ready to charge the Republic's flank.

choices.r: The cavalry sweeps across the snow and the Republican flank gives way. Nobody in Europe will see a charge like it again.

choices.t: Keep them back for the pursuit
choices.r: The horses wait behind the lines, steaming in the cold.

deck.title: The Sierra de Pàndols
deck.text: The battle has moved into the bare limestone hills above the Ebro. In the August heat, without shade or water, your infantry attack the same ridges again and again. The Republic's men are dug in among rocks too hard for picks.

choices.t: Bring water up by mule every night
choices.r: Long mule trains climb the tracks each night under fire.
Your guns fire more shells in a day than they did in a week at Madrid.
The ridges change hands, and change back.

deck.title: The Condor Legion is worn out
deck.text: The Condor Legion's commander reports that his aircraft are worn out. Berlin is thinking of bringing the Legion home before war comes in Europe, unless you pay what you owe.

choices.r: Berlin sends replacement aircraft and new pilots.
Berlin accepts, and keeps a careful list.

deck.title: An exchange of prisoners
deck.text: The International Committee of the Red Cross proposes an exchange of prisoners between the two sides: officers for officers, civilians for civilians.

choices.r: A few hundred prisoners cross the lines at the French border.
Your answer is that there is nothing to discuss with a government that does not exist.

deck.title: Deserters
deck.text: Some of the Asturian prisoners you drafted into your army have slipped across the Ebro at night to rejoin the Republic, taking their rifles with them.

choices.r: Officers watch the former prisoners day and night.
The suspect battalions are sent to guard the Pyrenees.

deck.title: Bread over Madrid
deck.text: Madrid is starving. Its people live on lentils, which they call Dr Negrín's resistance pills. Your propaganda chief suggests dropping bread on the city from your aircraft, with leaflets promising plenty after the war.

choices.r: Loaves wrapped in paper fall over Madrid. Some people eat them; others say they are poisoned.
Fewer ships reach the Republic's last ports.

deck.title: The Anti-Comintern Pact
deck.text: Germany, Italy and Japan invite you to join their Anti-Comintern Pact against international communism, and to keep it secret until the war is over.

choices.r: Your signature is added in secret. It will be announced in April.

choices.t: Wait until the war is won
choices.r: Berlin is disappointed but patient.

deck.title: The fifth column
deck.text: Your agents in Madrid report that many officers in the Republic's army are ready to change sides when the moment comes, and some are already talking to you through go-betweens.

choices.r: Word goes back through the lines that those who help end the war will be spared.
They will have to trust your generosity, which you have not promised.

deck.title: The camps
deck.text: With hundreds of thousands of prisoners in your hands, your inspectorate of concentration camps reports that its camps are overflowing: bullrings, monasteries and football grounds ringed with barbed wire.

choices.t: Classify the prisoners and release the harmless
choices.r: Committees sort the prisoners into the "recoverable" and the rest. Tens of thousands go home, under watch.
New camps open in old factories and convents.

deck.title: The Italians want a parade
deck.text: Mussolini wants his troops to march at the head of your victory parade, and the newsreels to show it.

choices.t: Give them the place of honour
choices.h: Italy pleased · your officers resent it
choices.r: Rome is delighted. Your officers are not.
The Italians will march, but behind the Legion and the Regulares.
